# Acts 15:21–41: Research notes

**v. 21**
- Ellicott: "for" gives James's reason for writing only to the Gentiles. Jews heard the Law every Sabbath and didn't need the instruction, which is why the letter goes only to Gentile believers (v. 23).  https://biblehub.com/acts/15-21.htm
- Barnes: the Law that forbids these things was read constantly. Jewish converts wouldn't quickly learn that the ceremonial law had ended, so it made sense not to offend them needlessly.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/15-21.html
- Calvin mentions a reading held by some interpreters: Jews already knew the Law, so the council asked only these few things of Gentiles, who had never carried that yoke.  (same URL)
- Gill offers two reasons. Gentiles hearing the Law expounded every week might think they had to keep all of it unless told they were free. And Jews had no cause to complain, because synagogue worship would carry on as before.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/15-21.htm
- Catholic Encyclopedia (catholic.com): Jewish Christians who heard these rules read in synagogue would be offended if Gentile believers ignored them.  https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/judaizers

**v. 22**
- Catholic Encyclopedia: James's proposal was adopted almost word for word. The decree went out from "the apostles and ancients, with the whole church" by way of two delegates, Judas and Silas.  https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08537a.htm

**v. 23**
- Ellicott: the letter is addressed only to Gentile believers.  https://biblehub.com/acts/15-21.htm

**v. 24**
- Pulpit Commentary: the letter is wise and careful. It leaves out the details of the debate and blames no one, yet quietly supports Paul's position.  https://biblehub.com/sermons/acts/15-28.htm

**v. 28**
- Traditional reading: the council saw the Spirit as guiding its decision.
  - Guzik: the unity behind the decision was evidence of the Spirit, who spoke through James and confirmed it through others.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/
  - Gill gives the signs: prayer, power in speaking, agreement with Scripture, and unanimity.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/15-28.html
  - Constable, quoting Kent: the Spirit usually leads through harmony among responsive people, not through miracles.  (same URL)
- **Where Protestant traditions differ: can later church councils claim the same authority?**
  - Reformed: Calvin says the phrase makes the Spirit the "captain, guide, and governor" of the decision. He argues it shows councils should decree nothing the Spirit hasn't given them.  (same URL). Barnes (Presbyterian) calls it "a strong and undoubted claim to inspiration."  (same URL)
  - Methodist: Benson says it can't be applied to church councils that have no inspired apostles leading them.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/15-28.htm. Clarke says the decree came from the Spirit's "especial inspiration."  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/15-28.html
  - Anglican: the Pulpit Commentary agrees with Bishop Wordsworth that councils today can't use these words when framing canons.  https://biblehub.com/acts/15-28.htm
  - Matthew Henry: the apostles' extraordinary gifts gave their decrees an authority no one can claim since those gifts ceased.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/15-28.html
  - Charismatic (Calvary Chapel): Chuck Smith sees the spiritual gift called the "word of wisdom" working through James.  (same URL)
- Catholic: the Catholic Encyclopedia says the council showed the apostles' "divinely founded right" to make church law for the people in their care.  https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/01067a.htm
- "Essential requirements": Ellicott thinks "necessary" was chosen because it fit both views. Pharisee Christians could read the rules as permanent, and Paul as a temporary, wise measure.  https://biblehub.com/acts/15-28.htm

**v. 29**
- **Where traditions differ: are the rules permanent or temporary?**
  - Baptist: Gill says they weren't needed for salvation. They were needed to keep peace among the churches, at least for that time.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wes/acts/15-28.html
  - Methodist: Clarke says they were needed for "all times, all places."  (same URL)
  - Reformed: Calvin says the food rules were things indifferent in themselves, singled out because they were linked to idolatry.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/15-20.html
- Why these four rules?
  - Constable thinks all four were tied to pagan worship, and the aim was unity between Jewish and Gentile believers.  (same URL)
  - Guzik: Gentiles weren't under the Law of Moses but were under "the Law of Love."  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/
  - GotQuestions: the rules weren't conditions of salvation. They were meant to keep peace in the early church.  https://www.gotquestions.org/Jerusalem-Council.html
- Catholic view:
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia links the four rules to Leviticus 17–18 and says they were given "for the sake of charity and union." It suggests "fornication" probably means marriages between close relatives.  https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/08537a.htm
  - The Council of Florence ruled that these food rules no longer bind as law.  https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/abstinence-food
- Seedbed (Wesleyan): one article argues that an important fact about the decree's link to the Law is being overlooked. Commenters dispute whether the four rules really match Leviticus.  https://seedbed.com/acts-15-doesnt-mean-think-means/

**v. 31**
- Matthew Henry: the comfort was hearing that "carnal ordinances" (outward religious rules) no longer applied to them, and that peace had returned to the church.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/15-34.htm

**v. 33**
- Light of Israel commentary: "they" means both Judas and Silas went back to Jerusalem.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/15-34.html

**v. 34 (textual question)**
- Barnes: the verse is missing from many manuscripts. A copyist probably added it to complete the story.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/15-34.htm
- JFB: it may have been added to explain v. 40.  (same URL)
- A. T. Robertson (quoted by Light of Israel): the "some days" of v. 36 gave Silas plenty of time to come back from Jerusalem.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/15-34.html
- Matthew Henry treats the verse as genuine and doesn't fault Silas.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Act/Act_015.cfm
- A Bible Hub study note defends it as fitting Luke's story.  https://biblehub.com/acts/15-34.htm

**v. 35**
- Matthew Henry: many others were working there too, and others' zeal should stir us up, not make us idle.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/15-34.htm

**v. 36**
- Bridgeway: they wanted to revisit the Galatian churches because of the recent trouble with the Judaizers.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/15-39.html

**vv. 37–38**
- Guzik: Mark had left under less than honourable circumstances (Acts 13:13), which probably made Paul unwilling to trust him.  He adds that the relationship may already have been strained after Barnabas sided with the Judaizers at Antioch (Galatians 2:13).  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/studyguide_act/act_15.cfm
- Deffinbaugh (bible.org): Barnabas was thinking mainly of Mark, Paul mainly of the mission.  https://bible.org/seriespage/24-when-division-becomes-multiplication-acts-153-1610

**v. 39: Who was right?**
- Neither side is clearly approved:
  - Guzik: Luke gives no clue. Where there is sharp contention someone is wrong, usually both sides.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-15/
  - Barclay: it's impossible to say.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/15-39.html
  - Matthew Henry blames both for their heat and stubbornness.  (same URL)
- Paul was right:
  - Wesley (Methodist): nothing says the sharpness was on both sides. Paul had the right on his side and probably kept it with love. Barnabas left the work.  (same URL)
  - JFB grants that later events might seem to favour Barnabas, but says Paul could judge only by Mark's past.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/15-39.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary mentions a writer who thought Paul too severe and domineering. It answers that this depends on whether the issue was really minor.  https://biblehub.com/acts/15-39.htm
- How serious was the split?
  - Constable: it was a strong disagreement, not personal dislike.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/15-39.html
  - Deffinbaugh: it came from different gifts and callings, not pride.  https://bible.org/seriespage/24-when-division-becomes-multiplication-acts-153-1610
  - The Cambridge Bible says the Greek word points to a short, sharp dispute rather than a long one.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/acts/15-39.htm
- God's providence:
  - The Geneva Study Bible says God uses his servants' faults to build the church, but warns against letting anger overflow.  (same URL)
  - The result was two mission teams instead of one.  (same URL)
  - TGC: Paul later spoke well of both men.  https://ca.thegospelcoalition.org/columns/straight-paths/when-christians-disagree/
- Catholic: Haydock calls it a dispute carried on with reasoning and argument.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/15-39.html

**v. 40**
- Themelios (TGC) rejects the idea that Paul was the less mature one. It points to the church commending Paul and Silas and the churches growing afterwards (15:40–41; 16:5).  https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/on-disagreements-in-ministry/

**v. 41**
- Bridgeway: Barnabas went home to Cyprus, and Paul went home to Cilicia with Silas.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/acts/15-39.html
